cognition.def: All the mental activity of knowing: perceiving, paying attention, thinking, remembering and using language.

perception.def: The process of organizing and interpreting sensory information so it has meaning. Sensation detects a stimulus; perception makes sense of it.

attention.def: Focusing mental resources on some information while ignoring the rest. It is limited, so what is not attended to may go unnoticed.

selective-attention.def: Focusing awareness on one stimulus or task while filtering out others, such as following one conversation in a noisy room.

cocktail-party.def: Noticing an important stimulus, such as your own name, among sounds you were ignoring. It shows that unattended input is still processed a little.

change-blindness.def: Failing to notice a change in a scene, such as a swapped object between two shots of a film.

inattentional-blindness.def: Failing to see an object in plain view because attention is on something else, as when people counting passes miss a person in a gorilla suit.

bottom-up.def: Perception that starts with the raw sensory features (lines, colors, edges) and builds them into a whole.

top-down.def: Perception guided by knowledge, expectations and experience, such as reading a messy word from the sentence around it.

schema.def: A mental framework that organizes knowledge about something (a restaurant, a dog, a first day of school) and shapes what we expect and notice.

perceptual-set.def: A readiness to perceive something in a certain way, set up by expectations, context, recent experience or emotion.

gestalt.def: The idea that the brain organizes sensations into meaningful wholes; the whole is different from the sum of its parts. The Gestalt principles describe how parts are grouped.

closure.def: The Gestalt tendency to fill in gaps so that an incomplete outline is seen as a whole object.

figure-ground.def: The organization of a scene into an object (the figure) that stands out from its surroundings (the ground).

proximity.def: The Gestalt tendency to group things that are close together.

similarity.def: The Gestalt tendency to group things that look alike in color, shape or size.

depth-perception.def: The ability to see the world in three dimensions and judge distance, from binocular and monocular cues.

binocular-cue.def: A depth cue that needs both eyes: retinal disparity and convergence.

retinal-disparity.def: A binocular cue: the two eyes see slightly different images of a scene, and the bigger the difference, the closer the object.

convergence.def: A binocular cue: the eyes turn inward to look at a near object, and the brain reads the amount of turning as distance.

monocular-cue.def: A depth cue that works with one eye, such as relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient and relative clarity.

relative-clarity.def: A monocular cue: hazy, blurry objects are seen as farther away than sharp, clear ones.

relative-size.def: A monocular cue: of two objects thought to be the same size, the one with the smaller image is seen as farther away.

texture-gradient.def: A monocular cue: surface detail looks coarse and spread out up close and finer and denser in the distance.

linear-perspective.def: A monocular cue: parallel lines, like railroad tracks, seem to meet in the distance.

interposition.def: A monocular cue: an object that blocks part of another is seen as closer.

perceptual-constancy.def: Perceiving objects as unchanging in size, shape and color even as the image on the retina or the lighting changes.

apparent-movement.def: Perceiving motion in a rapid series of still images, as in a movie or a row of blinking lights (the phi phenomenon).
